newsitem.title: USA: GE labor pact cost pegged at extra $1 bln.
newsitem.headline: GE labor pact cost pegged at extra $1 bln.

text.p: The labor settlement between General Electric Co and its unions is expected to cost the company an additional $1 billion over the life of the contract, said Ed Fire, who led the bargaining for the 14 unions negotiating a new contract.

The three year pact expired at midnight on June 29, but terms of the contract, which include improved early retirement provisions and an 8.75 percent wage increase over three years, were not made public until today.
He said that while the unions did not achieve all of its aims, he expected that the contract would be overwhelmingly ratified in voting that will take place next week.
"We are recommending ratification for a contract that is the richest in the history of collective bargaining," said Fire in comments at a press conference Thursday morning.
A GE spokesman could not confirm the $1 billion cost of the contract, but said that both sides in the talks had wanted to keep the company competitive.
"(The year 2000) will be another tough negotiation," said the spokesman. "It's always tough. The relationships are good, but the negotiations are tough."

The unions did not receive the iron-clad guarantee that all jobs would be protected. But it did, said Fire, get a provision that allows workers with 30 years experience to retire from certain plants, regardless of age. The company would then hire new workers, he said.
"These people will be replaced," said Fire of the 10,000 affected workers, citing the provision as a victory for job preservation, the most important issue for the unions.

He also said the two sides agreed on a Jobs Preservation Committe to work locally on job security issues. "It's going to be a real opportunity," he said. "Local management is just as interested in preserving jobs as local unions."

The unions made only partial gains on another of its chief positions. They had wanted GE to remain neutral during organizing drives, but settled for a "Code of Conduct" in which, in essence, both sides will be allowed to make their views known, but both sides will also refrain from personal attacks during organizing drives.
The company is currently facing union organizing drives in three plants in the South, said Fire.
GE stock was among the 25 most heavily traded issues on the New York Stock Exchange Thursday. In early afternoon trading shares changed hands at 69-1/16, up 1-1/2 from Wednesday's close.
